paras: The Wheeling gas works strike was a work stoppage in January 1881 in which white stokers and chargers at the Gas Works in Wheeling, West Virginia, refused to work after a Black fireman was hired and were replaced by Black workers. No violence was reported, and a rumor that the strikers would interfere with the works came to nothing. The city's two dailies treated it mainly as a dispute over why the men struck, argued in signed cards into early February.

According to Superintendent J. M. Dillon, on the day before Christmas 1880 the men threatened to stop work unless he added two men to each turn, and he gave in. Dillon wrote that about a week later he shut the small retort house and "quietly dropped" the leaders of that strike, then hired two Black men "who had been for years firemen on the river" to ease the stokers' heavier work. The strikers said instead that when the western retort house closed, two white workers, John Flaherty and Jacob Heyburn, were discharged, and two Black men were then hired.

The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reported that a Black man was hired as a fireman on Tuesday, January 11, and that on Wednesday evening the night turn refused to work unless he was let go. Dillon gave way for that night, but the Gas Works trustees ratified the hiring, and the fireman returned to work on Thursday. When the night turn again refused that evening, "a large number of negroes was at once set to work in the places of the strikers."

Secretary Harry Caldwell spent several hours at the works that evening, and a reporter found all quiet at ten o'clock. Dillon told the reporter that nearly all of the fourteen men had quit, that he had put ten Black men in their places, and that he would take none of the strikers back. The Wheeling Register said trouble had been threatened that night but everything passed off quietly, the reported plan of the strikers to interfere proving groundless.

On January 14 a committee of four strikers called on the Register, which printed the names, nationality and politics of the eleven men who struck. They said the works were now run by two white and twelve Black men, and Flaherty said Dillon had once warned him about voting the Democratic ticket. No report of arrests or court proceedings appears in the coverage.

On January 27, the morning of a city election, the Intelligencer printed a card from Dillon saying an effort was under way to remove him and restore his predecessor on the ground that he had treated white men unjustly. Dillon denied that anyone had been discharged to make room for the Black men, said he had then employed nine Black men. Flaherty answered in the Register that Dillon's card contradicted itself and that the real leader of the strike was still at work. On February 4 both papers printed a card from the late superintendent denying any part in the strike and charging that men had been discharged over "creed and politics."

The Intelligencer headlined its first report "Strike at the Gas Works" with the deck "The Stokers and Chargers Refuse to Work with Negroes," described the men as "certain Hibernians," and said "the whole party rebelled." Its later columns carried Dillon's card under the heading "Color at the Gas Works," quoting the strikers' demand with a slur.

The Register's first item was brief and balanced the men's complaint of a "Cheap John arrangement" against the trustees' view that the men "seemed to think they owned the works." The next day it printed "The Strikers' Side," in which the men called the Intelligencer's article "brainless" for its "Hibernians" remark and insisted they had struck only for their discharged comrades.

The Intelligencer and Dillon said the men struck against working with Black men, while the strikers and Flaherty said they struck because white men were discharged to make places for Black men. Counts of the Black workers also differ: one fireman and then ten replacements in the Intelligencer's first report, two and then nine in Dillon's card, and twelve by the strikers' count.

bases: White stokers and chargers struck against the hiring of Black firemen and were replaced by Black workers, with no violence reported (A1, A2, A5).
The Intelligencer and Register independently reported the strike and the replacement by Black workers (A1, A2, A3), though they differ on its cause.

accounts.label: Intelligencer local report
accounts.gist: Night-turn stokers and chargers refused to work with a Black fireman, struck two evenings running, and were replaced by ten Black men; all was quiet.

accounts.label: Register local report
accounts.gist: Men were discharged and replaced with negroes, a strike followed, and a rumor that strikers would interfere proved groundless.

accounts.label: Strikers' committee
accounts.gist: They struck because white workers were discharged to make room for Black men, not against working with Black men; the works now ran with two white and twelve Black men.

accounts.label: Superintendent Dillon
accounts.gist: He hired two Black river firemen as additions to the force; the white men demanded their discharge with a slur, struck twice, and he then employed nine Black men.

accounts.label: John Flaherty
accounts.gist: Dillon's card was contradictory: men were dropped and Black men hired in their places, and the real strike leader remained employed.

framing.detail: The Intelligencer headlined that the stokers 'Refuse to Work with Negroes', said 'the whole party rebelled', and called the strikers 'certain Hibernians'.
The Register gave both the men's 'Cheap John' complaint and the trustees' view, then printed 'The Strikers' Side' and Flaherty's reply.

record_check.dossier: Dated local reports of Jan. 14 exist; Dillon dropped leaders of the earlier Dec. 24 strike, hired two Black firemen, and after two strikes replaced the strikers with nine or ten Black men
